canberra.title: Thousands of Canberra’s green thumbs converge on Commonwealth Park for a piece of Floriade
canberra.snippet: Floriade ended yesterday, but thousands flocked to Commonwealth Park this morning to take home a lasting piece of this year’s sprin...
canberra.content:
Thousands of Canberrans took home a piece of Floriade in the Great Big Bulb Dig. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

Floriade ended yesterday, but thousands flocked to Commonwealth Park this morning to take home a lasting piece of this year’s springtime festival.

Officially called the Great Big Bulb Dig, it gave local gardeners the opportunity to fit as many of the festival’s flowers as they could into an official Floriade tote bag.

Each bag cost $20, with the money raised from bag sales being donated to YWCA Canberra.

With a lofty fundraising target of $100,000, and over 2000 people ready to go through the gates as soon as they opened, YWCA CEO Frances Crimmins said she was confident the target would well and truly be met.

“While this day is a lot of fun and everyone gets to take a bulb home, it also allows us to raise money to deliver homes for vulnerable women and children who are impacted by domestic and family violence,” Ms Crimmins said.

“It’s a fantastic event at the end of a very successful festival, and it’s just delightful to see families coming out. It’s free to come in with your children and, as long as you have a bag, you’ll be able to take something home with you.”

Jenny, Kylie and Susan travelled all the way from Brisbane to get their own bulbs. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

Geoff and Erika were some of the very first through the gates.

The Great Big Bulb Dig was a family affair.

While Canberrans made up the majority of eager green thumbs, people from across the country joined in, digging up and taking home their own bulbs, including Jenny, Kylie and Susan, who flew all the way from Brisbane to take part in the Great Big Bulb Dig.

“We’d heard about Floriade for years and years. We had always wanted to come down and be a part of it,” Susan said.

“It’s crazy the number of people who have come down today, but when you see how beautiful the bulbs are, you can understand why so many people want to take just a little bit home,” Kylie continued.

“It’s just a great idea as well. It’s better to give the bulbs to people who will look after them and let them continue to grow instead of just letting them be mulched,” Jenny said.

Events ACT executive branch manager Ross Triffit said seeing the thousands of people pick their own bulbs was a beautiful end to a tremendous festival.

“All of these bulbs that have been here throughout Floriade are going to great homes spread across the backyards of Canberra,” he said.

“Even with heavy rain, high winds and even hail, we’ve seen a tremendous amount of visitors and a lot of great local community support.

“Today is the final chapter of the festival where we can help raise some important funds for YWCA, give the plants a new home and bring down the curtain.

“It really is the perfect end to what’s been another great Floriade.”

canberra.title: McBain says banks should be forced to wear card costs themselves
canberra.snippet: Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain says banks should be made to carry the cost of processing card payments themselves instead of...
canberra.content:
Labor frontbencher Kristy McBain says banks should not charge small businesses fees for point-of-sale transactions. Photo: James Coleman.

Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain says banks should be made to carry the cost of processing card payments themselves instead of passing them onto small businesses to absorb.

Businesses can no longer pass on card payment surcharges to customers, following new laws that took effect at the start of this month.

The surcharge ban covers eftpos, Visa and Mastercard, and includes credit, debit and prepaid cards.

The new rule was introduced following the RBA’s Review of Merchant Card Payment Costs and Surcharging, which found that removing the surcharges would support a more efficient and competitive payments system.

But Ms McBain wants the RBA to go further and stop banks charging small businesses surcharge fees for point-of-sale transactions.

“These banks are making billions of dollars in profits every year and small businesses are already paying account keeping fees and a range of other fees directly to their banks,” the minister said on Monday (12 October).

“I’d like to see the RBA actually take that next step and say, you know, there is no charging for those point of sale machines.”

While consumers have appreciated the surcharges on their card payments disappearing, there has been a massive backlash from the business sector.

Businesses now have to absorb the costs themselves or raise the prices of their goods and services, and some have already started doing so.

The issue was worsened by the fact that the Australian Tax Office refused to absorb the fees and decided not to accept credit card payments because of the surcharge ban.

Amid cries of hypocrisy from the business community, Treasurer Jim Chalmers stepped in last week to make the ATO delay its refusal of card payments.

The Coalition described it as a humiliating backdown for the Treasurer.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said on Monday that Ms McBain’s buy-in to the debate shows Labor continues to be all over the place on the surcharge ban, with little leadership shown by Anthony Albanese.

“Last week, the Prime Minister said that small businesses needed to absorb it, and then … we find out the Tax Office is not going to absorb it,” he said.

“She [Ms McBain] can say whatever she likes, but in the end, what we really need is this government to quit the hypocrisy, to scrap the ban on credit cards for small businesses by the ATO.

“Not delay it. A delay doesn’t cut it. Scrap it. And then we know you’re serious about actually having a real discussion about this. That’s what they need to do.”

The minister’s call for small businesses to be freed of the surcharge ban follows the Greens suggesting the same thing last week.

Greens deputy leader Steph Hodgins-May says the government could assist small businesses by putting the onus back onto banks.

She urged Labor to force the banking sector to absorb card transaction costs.

“Labor needs to put down rules that will protect business – small business who are already doing it incredibly tough at this point,” Senator Hodgins-May said.

“And also the greed of big banks – they need to regulate the banks.

“This falls back on Labor. It was as predictable, I’d say, as the sun rising.

“And they have a responsibility in the depths of a cost-of-living crisis to regulate the banks and ensure that this does not get pushed on to consumers and to small business.”

The government has defended the ban on card surcharges being transferred to consumers, saying they were costing them $1.6 billion a year.

It won’t say yet, however, how much forcing the ATO to delay refusing credit card payments until June next year will cost the government.

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino said that question will be answered in the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook (MYEFO) later this year.

“The costs are partly dependent on ongoing negotiations between the ATO and the credit card companies,” Mr Mulino said.

“Those conversations will hopefully yield benefits for the taxpayer, but … the final costs will be announced in my MYEFO.”

canberra.title: Local councils warn of ‘significant impact’ after proposals to slash federal funding
canberra.snippet: Anger and frustration are growing in councils across NSW after the Local Government Grants Commission (LGGC) indicated that almost half o...
canberra.content:
The Executive Board of the Country Mayors Association of NSW. Chair Rick Firman (fourth from right) has written to the NSW Grants Commission to express MMA members’ concerns. Photo: Country Mayors Association of NSW.

Anger and frustration are growing in councils across NSW after the Local Government Grants Commission (LGGC) indicated that almost half of all NSW councils would receive less from the annual untied federal funding from 1 July 2027.

Known as Financial Assistance (FA) grants, they help local councils deliver services to their communities.

The annual FA grants are given by the federal government but administered by the state government, and councils are free to use these untied funds at their discretion.

But the total FA grant pool has been steadily decreasing.

In 1996, it represented 1 per cent of NSW tax revenue, but now the 128 councils across NSW share 0.49 per cent. Calls have been made to increase the rate as councils face rising infrastructure costs, along with cost-shifting by the NSW Government through additional responsibilities.

But far from seeing any sign of increase, some councils are facing the possibility of even less money coming their way after a new method of allocating the FA grants was proposed by the LGGC, which makes recommendations to the Office of Local Government about the distribution of the FA grants.

The move to reallocate the same pot of money, but give more to some councils at the expense of others, is shaping up to be a major battle, with councils writing to the LGGC to express their frustration at the methodology and lack of transparency.

Bega Valley Shire Council faces a decrease of almost $4 million, from $10.030 million to $6.187 million, a reduction of $3.843 million per annum, or 38.3 per cent.

BVSC has lodged a freedom of information request to learn more about the methodology.

“I believe this methodology will be very volatile,” Mayor Russell Fitzpatrick said.

“If you have a disaster and get grant income, it will be averaged over four years and affect the amount of the financial assistance grant.”

Mayor of Snowy Monaro Regional Council, Chris Hanna, said council had been advised that Snowy Monaro could see a $5.1 million reduction in the FA grant delivered to the shire.

“If this methodology is put in place, council will have to raise more money locally or reduce the levels of services currently provided to the community. This is a significant impact. A reduction in Commonwealth funding of that magnitude cannot simply be absorbed,” Cr Hanna said.

"I believe this methodology will be very volatile and that's a real worry," said Mayor Russell Fitzpatrick of Bega Valley Shire Council. Photo: Denise Dion.

Wollongong City Council Lord Mayor Tania Brown has spoken to NSW Premier Chris Minns about council's concerns over a significant loss of funding from the FA grants. Photo: Wollongong City Council.

“The real concern is that the overall funding pool for councils is just not enough," said Mayor Kenrick Winchester of Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council. Photo: Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council.

"A reduction in Commonwealth funding of that magnitude cannot simply be absorbed," said Mayor of Cooma Monaro Regional Council Chris Hanna. Photo: Cooma Monaro Regional Council.

At Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council, Mayor Kenrick Winchester says the proposed funding cut is $1.9 million.

“While council is in support of a fair funding model for councils and it is good to review the methodology, the proposed new methodology has led to some perverse outcomes. No council should be worse off. The real concern is that the overall funding pool for councils is just not enough,” Cr Winchester said.

Shoalhaven City Council vowed to provide detailed written feedback to the LGCC after being told its FA grant allocation would be reduced from $16.2 million to $14 million.

“Shoalhaven has been united with councils across Australia in advocating for an increase in federal financial support to address growing infrastructure backlogs, rising service demands and the ongoing impact of cost shifting from state to local government,” acting Mayor Peter Wilkins said.

“This proposed change to the funding allocation is a slap in the face to the Shoalhaven community. At a time when we’re already under significant financial pressure and working hard to make every dollar count, taking millions of dollars away from our region is the exact opposite of what’s needed.”

The Lord Mayor of Wollongong City Council, Tania Brown, has personally raised concerns regarding the proposed changes with NSW Premier Chris Minns.

Wollongong received $23.8 million in funding for the 2025-26 financial year through the FA grant program, but under the proposed modelling, this allocation would drop to about $7.7 million from July 2027, a cut of more than 67 per cent.

Wollongong Council has made a submission to the LGGC that the modelling lacks adequate data or supporting information, as well as transparency, and provides no transition period, despite proposing significant funding cuts within a single budget cycle.

“Council has worked diligently over many years to be in a sound financial position, and you really do need to question any methodology that suggests a $16 million cut within a single budget cycle is warranted or manageable,” Cr Brown said.

The Canberra Region Joint Organisation (CRJO) represents 11 councils surrounding Canberra.

Of the 11 councils, four will receive increases under the proposed methodology – Eurobodalla, Yass Valley, Wagga Wagga (an associate member) and Goulburn Mulwaree – but seven will be worse off, including Wingecarribee by $2.7 million and Upper Lachlan Shire Council by $3.2 million.

CRJO as a group will be down by more than $15 million because of reduced FA grants.

The Country Mayors Association is also concerned about what it says is a lack of nuance in the new methodology.

“Given the diversity that is represented by the NSW Local Government sector, which encompasses the largest city in Australia to some of the smallest villages that stretches across beaches, deserts, snowfields and forests, using just two key drivers fails to account for that diversity,” chair of the CMA Rick Firman said in his letter.

The CMA is also concerned that receiving other tied grants for council work will affect the annual FA grant amount, making budgeting highly volatile. Along with individual councils, the CMA has raised the number of “unknowns” in the calculations underpinning the new methodology, adding that it cannot support its adoption.

“Our stance at this point is that the existing methodology should remain in place and that further work be undertaken on the new methodology to address the concerns of the sector. Strong feedback from our members is that the new methodology should not leave any council worse off than the application of the existing distribution methodology,” Mr Firman said.

Feedback to the LGGC closed on 9 October and will be considered in the coming weeks.

The new FA grant system is expected to commence on 1 July 2027, but given the strong feelings among so many councils, considerable lobbying is likely in the interim.

Original Article published by Denise Dion on About Regional.

canberra.title: Opportunistic burglar targets Cooleman Court day spa destroyed in car crash
canberra.snippet: A Cooleman Court therapeutic massage and day spa business is once again a crime scene, with a person stealing staff belongings left behin...
canberra.content:
12 October 2026

Join the conversation

2

Harmony Tree Therapeutic Massage and Day Spa in Cooleman Court is now boarded up. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

A Cooleman Court therapeutic massage and day spa business is once again a crime scene, with a person stealing staff belongings left behind after a car smashed into the shopfront.

Five people were injured when the vehicle ploughed into the Weston business on Friday (9 October). Most were trapped beneath the vehicle.

Harmory Tree owner Sukanya Loasoe recently gave birth to her second child and is now dealing not only with a significantly damaged business, but also a burglary.

“We couldn’t take [our] things out because the car had pushed everything towards the end [of the building], and everything was smashed,” she told Region through a friend.

“The car was still there, but the person … might have had more time [to be inside the premises]. He slowly came and took everything.”

A staff member’s phone, car keys, house keys and ATM card were taken from the business.

It’s understood the card has since been used by the perpetrator.

The day spa’s insurer has now boarded up the shopfront, and ACT Policing officers were on scene this morning (12 October).

Two staff members were injured in Friday’s incident. One was in surgery for a second time today as a result of the accident.

Ms Loasoe was relieved everyone was alive.

“It’s sad, shocking,” she said.

“The Weston community has been helping … next we need to speak with the insurer and go from there.”

Five people were injured when a car crashed into the front of the Cooleman Court business. Photo: Ruby Garrety.

In a social media post, Canberrans were thanked for their support.

“This has been an incredibly difficult and stressful time for us and our staff. We are doing our best to deal with the damage and get through these challenging circumstances,” it read.

“We sincerely hope things will get better soon. Thank you to everyone for your kindness, understanding, and support. We truly appreciate it.”

An ACT Policing spokesperson confirmed it was investigating the incident.

“About 1:10 pm on Sunday (11 October) police received a report regarding a burglary at a shopfront at Cooleman Court shopping centre in Weston,” they said.

“Multiple items were allegedly stolen.”

Anyone with information has been asked to contact Crime Stoppers, quoting reference 8524827.

canberra.title: When creativity meets dissent: Canberra’s design festival returns to challenge the ordinary
canberra.snippet: What do a human-powered machine that can travel across land and water, a sustainable home, a repaired garment and a street performance ha...
canberra.content:
Increments by artist Matt Curtis is among the artworks featured at the Craft + Design Canberra Festival. Photo: Rob Little.

What do a human-powered machine that can travel across land and water, a sustainable home, a repaired garment and a street performance have in common?

They are all ways of challenging conventional thinking, and they will come together at this year’s Craft + Design Canberra Festival.

From unusual inventions racing across land, sand and Lake Burley Griffin to open homes, fashion, art and performances, the festival will explore how creativity can challenge the way we live, consume and interact with our surroundings.

With more than 130 events featuring over 500 creatives, the festival runs from 5 to 15 November under the theme Dissent, inviting Canberrans to look at familiar things differently. The festival will turn galleries, homes, streets, studios and public spaces into places for people to explore, question and create.

And while some events are ticketed, much of the program is free, with activities for families, art lovers, architecture enthusiasts, fashion followers and those simply curious about the city around them.

For Craft + Design Canberra CEO and artistic director Jodie Cunningham, dissent is not necessarily about protest or confrontation. It is about questioning accepted ways of doing things and imagining something better.

“We chose the theme of Dissent to reflect the state of the world, to challenge, and to offer hope,” Ms Cunningham told Region.

“At its best, dissent is an act of care. You dissent because you believe something better is possible.

“A repaired garment is an act of dissent. A house designed to need less energy is an act of dissent. A quilt stitched by a hundred hands is an act of dissent. A sculpture made of recycled glass is an act of dissent,” Ms Cunningham said.

The theme also reflects the experience of Black Summer and the role creativity and community connections can play during difficult times.

Ms Cunningham said the festival was shaped by concerns about climate change and the state of the world, but its response was deliberately creative rather than despairing.

One of the festival’s more unusual events is the Canberra Kinetic Sculpture Race at the National Carillon, where teams will put their handmade, human-powered creations to the test across land, sand and water.

Part artwork and part vehicle, the machines reflect the festival’s theme by challenging conventional ideas of transport, engineering and public art.

Architecture enthusiasts can explore award-winning sustainable homes through Canberra Open Homes, including an energy-positive house in Turner, a fully electric home in Deakin and a renovated Ainslie cottage.

Tours will also include the new CIT campus in Woden and the Australian War Memorial’s new entrance.

Sustainability runs through the program, from fashion workshops and markets challenging fast fashion to exhibitions exploring how discarded materials can be given new life.

More than 40 artists will open their studios, while hands-on workshops will give visitors an opportunity to try different crafts.

At Canberra Contemporary, Hal Fitzpatrick’s Craftivism exhibition explores how textiles and traditional craft practices can become tools for social commentary.

“Artists use thread, glass, clay and metal to say something about the world, and the work asks us to stop, look and think,” Ms Cunningham said.

Performance also takes dissent beyond galleries. Canberra Youth Theatre will collaborate with a Canadian group on a production moving through city streets, while ALTER at Belconnen Arts Centre brings together dancers living with and without disability to explore identity and inclusion.

Symposiums will explore how design can tackle housing and climate challenges, and whether Canberra measures its success in the right ways. Exhibitions will range from recycled glass art and contemporary jewellery to the design of Australia’s coins.

Beyond the individual events, the festival reflects Canberra’s ambition to gain recognition through UNESCO’s Creative Cities Network.

Ms Cunningham said the bid drew on the capital’s architectural heritage, First Nations design traditions and contemporary creative industries, positioning design as part of everyday life rather than something confined to galleries.

The festival will begin with a free opening celebration in Civic Square on Thursday 5 November, featuring a smoking ceremony, live music and the announcement of the Robert Foster Metal Prize winners.

The 2024 festival attracted more than 140,000 visits and public art encounters, including around 90,000 direct attendees. Organisers expect this year’s larger program to draw substantial crowds, although individual workshops and talks will have limited capacities.

For visitors unsure where to begin, the festival website offers curated itineraries organised around interests such as architecture, design and free activities.

The full program, ticket details and free-event listings are available at craftanddesigncanberrafestival.org.

australia.title: More part-time bosses and co-CEOs could keep women in leadership and narrow Australia’s pay gap
australia.snippet: Uneven caring responsibilities combined with a lack of flexible work options have prevented women from staying in senior positions, resea...
australia.content:
More part-time bosses and “co-CEOs” could keep women in leadership and narrow Australia’s gender pay gap, the federal government’s Workplace Gender Equality Agency says.

WGEA warned resistance to gender equality was growing and urged employers to make management more flexible to reduce the gender pay gap, where women earn $0.79 for every $1 a man makes on average.

WGEA and Curtin University research on Tuesday found women were reaching senior positions but were more likely to leave, widening the pay gap and contributing to under-representation in high-paying and senior roles.

Full-time women were promoted more often than men in 2024-25, according to the report’s analysis of WGEA data covering 5.4 million employees.

But men were slightly more likely to be promoted to management positions and women who reached management positions were more likely to resign than their male counterparts, at 13.8% compared to 12%.

WGEA’s chief executive, Christine Castley, said uneven caring responsibilities combined with a lack of flexible work options had prevented women from staying in senior positions.

“There is very much an embedded idea that management roles can never be part-time, and probably what flows from that is most flexible arrangements don’t apply to management roles,” Castley said.

Most women still either stop working or work part-time after having their first child, according to the report’s analysis of Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (Hilda) data.

Leadership could be dominated by men even in industries where most workers were women, the report found.

In the health care and social assistance sector, women made up three-quarters of the workforce but about half of CEO positions. Women accounted for just one in five board chairs or chief executives of Australian companies.

Castley said employers could think creatively about reforms to keep women in senior roles, including allowing grandparents to access carer’s leave or rostering to fit school drop-off and pickup.

“We’re seeing increasingly the use of – even at the CEO level – co-CEOs, who are essentially job sharing a role.”

The report found that just 13.2% of organisations designed management roles for part-time work but those that did saw significantly higher promotion rates for female part-time non-managers.

Employers with flexible work strategies tended to employ more women at every level of senior management.

Dr Silvia Salazar, a report co-author, said parents sharing care responsibility would also play a role.

Women accounted for 80% of people taking primary carer parental leave in 2024-25 and were more likely to quit their job while on parental leave than men.

The report found 33% employers were not funding additional paid parental leave.

“Employers cannot determine how care is divided at home, but they can help make sure that becoming a parent does not mean stepping off the path to career progression,” Salazar said.

Workplace equality metrics have improved in recent years but policies addressing gendered inequality have faced growing hostility, especially among Australian youth.

The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, has said the gender pay gap is due to women taking time off but employers should not have to pay for parental leave.

Castley said the agency aimed to provide objective data in the face of growing scepticism over gender equity.

“Certainly many people who have worked in this space have a bit of a sense that the conversation’s moved a few steps backwards from where it was,” Castley said.

“We have made really good progress over the last 40 years or so in this context, but now there is a narrative that seems to be pulling that progress backwards, at least in a narrative sense.”

australia.title: ‘BYD effect’: electric vehicle boom becomes unexpected tool to combat inflation
australia.snippet: More and more Australian consumers are expected to ‘unplug themselves from the oil shock’ with at least five EVs priced around or below $...
australia.content:
Electric vehicle sales are surging in Australia, powering a transition that goes beyond fuel savings to become an unexpected tool to combat high inflation.

The abrupt shift away from petrol and diesel vehicles, accelerated by elevated fuel costs caused by the Iran conflict, is being supported by an influx of cheaper EVs that is reducing associated costs such as insurance.

Chris Dickman, senior portfolio manager at fund manager Australian Ethical, describes the trend as the “BYD effect”, referring to the low-priced Chinese vehicles which he says are an unexpected disinflationary force.

Dickman says that by helping drivers use less petrol, and bringing down the cost of new and used cars, EV uptake is blunting the impact of high oil prices across the economy.

“There are more and more consumers who are trying to unplug themselves from the oil shock,” Dickman says.

He says the rise of EVs is an example of how newer, cleaner technology eventually outcompetes incumbents on pure economics as they gain popularity and market size.

Virtually all of the EV cost impediments of a few years ago – including high sticker prices, inadequate charging networks, elevated insurance premiums and expensive servicing, battery and parts replacements – are reversing as Australia’s market matures.

NRMA’s car ownership report found that there are now at least five EVs priced around or below the $30,000 mark, all of which are Chinese brands.

Fuelling the shift

While EVs and hybrids have been gaining traction for years, the US-Israel war on Iran and subsequent oil price spike accelerated demand in March, and it has continued largely unabated.

Battery EV sales now account for almost 25% of new vehicle sales, according to Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries data. About half of all new sales are either EVs or hybrids, and more EVs were sold last month than petrol-only cars.

The EV-focused Chinese brands BYD, GWM, Chery, Geely and MG were all in the top 10 biggest selling automakers in Australia in September. Three years ago, only MG featured in that list.

Adam Triggs, co-founder at economics consulting group Mandala Partners, said the next step towards protecting Australia from oil shocks was to electrify diesel-dependent freight networks.

“When we look at light commercial vehicles, those are the little trucks that sort of fly around the streets, they already have a total cost of ownership that is very competitive against their fossil fuel counterparts, and we would expect those to be the first to go electric,” he says.

Diesel prices have now surpassed $2.80 a litre at many petrol stations, while unleaded has pushed past $2.40/L in most state capital cities, according to Australian Institute of Petroleum data.

The high fuel prices are rattling the Australian economy, elevating costs across nearly all goods and services and overshadowing the deflationary effect of the EV transition.

Last month, the Reserve Bank lifted its key interest rate to 4.6%, its highest level since 2011, and warned of further hikes as the unending Iran conflict pushes prices “permanently higher”.

Triggs says there’s a role for the government to help offset the upfront costs of electrifying Australia’s freight networks.

“What’s happened over time is once you’ve got a critical mass, you end up seeing costs fall dramatically,” Triggs said.

“It’s the same for trucks. There are some practical things for the government to do over the next five to 10 years to start getting the freight fleet electrified, and then the market will take over from there.”

australia.title: Rescued turtles return home after NSW government cut flows to wetland
australia.snippet: Environmental water to the area was halted after a complaint from a private landholder, leading to the deaths of wildlife and sheep Get o...
australia.content:
Freshwater turtles rescued from a dried-up water hole in western New South Wales after the state government cut environmental water to the area are being returned home.

Late last month, 10 broad-shelled turtles and three Murray River turtles were released back into the Gingham water hole in the state’s Gwydir region.

In what the environment minister, Penny Sharpe, described as a “remarkable conservation outcome”, 281 eggs from rescued turtles are also incubating at Taronga zoo in Dubbo.

The rapidly drying water hole was the site of a rescue mission in April after University of New England scientists raised the alarm that an “incomprehensible” environmental catastrophe was unfolding.

WaterNSW had stopped environmental flows to the area, after a complaint from a private landholder, leading to the deaths of turtles, birds, frogs and sheep.

Environmental flows refer to water released by the government from dams and tributaries into rivers and ecosystems to maintain or restore their health.

The situation sparked outcry after scientist Deb Bower spoke publicly to Guardian Australia, with footage taken by NSW Greens water spokesperson Cate Faehrmann showing the researchers digging through mud to find surviving turtles.

Thirty-nine turtles were taken into care at Taronga zoo in Dubbo. In May, the government expedited legislation to clearly protect WaterNSW from liability claims when delivering environmental flows, and the water was turned back on.

Six months on, the Gingham water hole is full once more and the first group of 13 surviving turtles have been returned to their habitat.

“That’s what we work for as conservation scientists – to be able to get animals back into the wild,” said Dr Phoebe Meagher, a wildlife conservation officer at Taronga Conservation Society.

Meagher said of the 39 turtles, two had to be humanely euthanised. She said the remaining 37 turtles were healthy enough to be rehabilitated.

She said the 24 turtles that were still in care were expected to return by the end of the year, pending health checks.

Many of the turtles rescued in April had been carrying eggs. Meagher said zoo staff made a decision to induce the animals for welfare reasons and 281 eggs were being housed in incubators, with the hatchlings expected early next year.

Meagher said not all of the eggs would hatch successfully but the zoo hoped to release any hatchlings back at the Gingham water hole when they were ready.

Photos and video of the adult turtles being released late last month showed a much healthier site than the parched environment that confronted researchers in May.

“When those animals got brought to us, it was a pretty dire situation,” Meagher said.

“To be able to see those photos of how good it looks and see the turtles being released back to their home, that’s what we work for as conservation scientists

“To be able to even further boost that population with hatchlings, it’s why we do what we do.”

Sharpe said conservation “isn’t always about following a set playbook”.

“Sometimes a crisis creates an opportunity to do something truly groundbreaking,” she said.

“By rescuing these turtles and safeguarding more than 250 eggs, we’ve turned a potential loss into a remarkable opportunity for species recovery.”

Faehrmann said she was “incredibly relieved to see that some of the turtles have started to be released back into the Gwydir wetlands”.

“This is a good news story but not because of the efforts of the government, despite what their media release says,” she said.

“It wasn’t until the Guardian published its story with the footage I provided of the turtles being dug up out of the mud that the government swung into action.

“It shouldn’t have taken the courage of the UNE researchers and a viral video to get the government to act, but that’s what was needed.”

She said she had been “kept up at night” wondering how many other wetlands and wildlife were suffering because there was not enough water for the environment.

Faehrmann recently returned from a trip to the Ramsar-listed Macquarie Marshes and said the area desperately needed more flows.

australia.title: Julie Inman Grant may be able to limit Australians seeing a livestreamed US execution – but it could start a diplomatic incident
australia.snippet: A history of tech giant legal challenges and US political criticism shows there’s no easy solution for the eSafety commissioner Get our n...
australia.content:
Australia’s online safety regulator has a few levers to limit the public seeing the US’s planned livestream of an execution, but history suggests it will lead to a very public fight.

The US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, announced last week the planned execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan would be livestreamed when the military execution is carried out in early December.

The Greens have called on the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, and the Albanese government to ensure that the event – if it goes ahead and is livestreamed – is not seen by Australians on TV or their devices.

The eSafety commissioner, under the Online Safety Act, has powers to order platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and X to block Australians from accessing posts that contain content deemed to be “refused classification” under Australian classification law.

The classification of such extreme violent material is typically applied to content online of terror attacks and other terror-related content, but it could be applied to clips of the video of the public execution after the fact.

While some companies like Meta will probably apply their own terms of service and prevent the distribution of the video, history suggests others will take a stand that the video should remain on their platforms.

X has given no indication whether it will allow such videos, but the platform owned by Elon Musk has a long history of legal challenges against eSafety when it comes to this sort of content.

In 2024, X was successful in allowing footage of the stabbing of a Sydney bishop in his church in 2024 to remain available to Australians – the platform even recruited the bishop, Mar Mari Emmanuel, to argue to the court to allow the footage to stay online.

Most recently, X won an appeal to the classifications review board to have the classification of the video of the assassination of rightwing influencer Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University downgraded from RC to R18+, after eSafety ordered the removal of clips of the assassination last year.

It also won a similar case to reduce the rating of videos of the attack on Iryna Zarutska on a train in Charlotte, North Carolina in August last year down to R18+.

In laws passed by the former Coalition government in 2019 in the wake of the Christchurch terror attack, the eSafety commissioner also has powers to issue takedown notices to websites hosting footage that, among other things, depicts “actual violent crime such as murder, attempted murder, rape, torture”.

These laws were developed with the view to block streaming of terror attacks, but could have wider applications for state-sponsored violence such as executions.

The eSafety commissioner last used these powers in 2022 to order websites to remove videos and related materials of the Buffalo, New York terrorist attack in 2022. It can also declare an “online crisis event” and order internet service providers such as Telstra and Optus to block sites hosting the content, but this power has yet to be used.

The ISPs complied with eSafety’s request to block sites hosting the Christchurch attack in 2019 before the parliament had passed the laws.

Such a move – particularly if focused on large social media platforms, or potentially sites owned by the Trump administration – may lead to a domestic firestorm among conservative media as well as a potential diplomatic incident, and may not be the regulator’s preferred option – especially given it has not been used before.

Last, there is the potential to seek penalties against platforms that fail to detect and remove violent material from their platform. The regulator is now testing this law out with messaging platform Telegram, which eSafety has alleged failed to remove some content that included executions conducted by terrorist groups.

The eSafety commissioner is seeking fines of up to A$54.6m, and the hearing for the case is set down for February next year.

The other factor to consider is the laser focus some in the US already have on Inman Grant. Her term is up in January next year, and Inman Grant has previously said she will not seek another term, but Trump-aligned politicians such as the Republican congressman Jim Jordan have labelled Inman Grant as a “zealot for global takedowns” and claimed she has threatened American speech on social media platforms.

Inman Grant has rejected the claims, and she declined an invitation to speak before a US congress hearing at the time.

If Inman Grant bears the responsibility for decisions around whether Australians can see the livestreamed execution, it will likely provoke a new round of criticism.

The regulator has not indicated what it would do in the event the execution is livestreamed, but the history of legal challenges and attention from the right of politics in the US suggests no easy solution in the eSafety toolkit – short of ministerial intervention.

australia.title: Australian democracy campaigner detained in Vietnam on alleged terrorism offences uncontactable, wife says
australia.snippet: Tran Hiep spent his 51st birthday alone in a notorious detention centre in Ho Chi Minh City after his sudden arrest last month Get our br...
australia.content:
Tran Hiep spent his 51st birthday alone in a notorious detention centre in Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh City after his sudden arrest last month.

The Melbourne-based Vietnamese-Australian democracy campaigner hasn’t been heard from since mid-September when Vietnamese authorities detained him for alleged terrorism and forging identity documents.

The alarm was first raised by his wife, Chloe Dang, when Hiep failed to board his flight from the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh, on 18 September where he was meeting with human rights defenders.

For nearly a fortnight, Hiep had apparently vanished. Then the Vietnamese authorities confirmed he was in jail, awaiting trial.

More than three weeks later, Dang has been told by Australian authorities Hiep is being held in the B34 pre-trial detention centre in Ho Chi Minh City, known for alleged human rights abuses against political prisoners.

“I will not stop worrying until I hear from him or see him with my own eyes,” Dang said.

“Last week, he had to spend his birthday alone in detention. We always do everything together, so the thought of that is truly heartbreaking for me.”

Dang wants his immediate and unconditional release.

Not the only detainee

Hiep is the latest Australian human rights campaigner to be detained in Vietnam.

Vietnamese-born Australian, Chau Van Kham, was arrested in Vietnam in January 2019 and sentenced to 12 years’ imprisonment on “financing terrorism” charges over his membership of the pro-democracy group Viet Tan. He was released after four years in 2023.

Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, is also accused of being a member of Viet Tan – which Vietnam describes as a terrorist group.

Human Rights Watch has previously described Viet Tan as “an opposition political party … which operates openly and lawfully in many countries including Australia, but which Hanoi arbitrarily labels ‘terrorist’”.

According to a Vietnamese government statement, Hiep was arrested entering Vietnam from the Cambodian border along with another human rights activist, Nguyen Duc Thuan, who is also Vietnamese and holds a Norwegian passport.

A third person, Thai Cong Truong Son, was also arrested. Cambodian authorities have since denied any involvement in the arrest or detainment of the three men, who, they say, were intercepted at the My Quy Tay border crossing.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is providing the family with consular assistance but won’t comment on his case due to privacy obligations.

The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said she had made personal representations regarding Hiep’s case but would be “careful what I say publicly”.

“We know that different political regimes in the region have very different approaches to individual freedom and political freedom to that Australia takes,” Wong told ABC on Friday.

‘Worsening human rights situation’

Human rights advocates are concerned Australia’s silence in the public arena is the wrong approach while Hiep remains uncontactable, and his condition unknown.

Kyinzom Dhongdue, Amnesty International Australia’s strategy and efficacy manager, said the human rights group was “increasingly concerned about the worsening human rights situation in Vietnam”.

Dang, as well as Hiep’s lawyer Alison Battisson, Amnesty, Human Rights Watch, and other groups, believe Hiep was abducted by Vietnamese authorities while in Cambodia. If so, his arrest would be a violation of international law.

“This is an egregious case of transnational oppression in which an Australian citizen has been kidnapped from a third country – Cambodia – and forcibly taken to Vietnam,” Battisson claimed.

Both Vietnamese and Cambodian authorities deny this happened.

Dhongdue said the Australian government should demand an independent investigation, noting previous cases.

“I think the government really needs to speak out publicly, privately, at the highest level, because keeping it quiet doesn’t help,” Dhongdue said.

Kylie Moore-Gilbert was held in Iranian detention from September 2018 for 804 days until her eventual release in November 2020.

Moore-Gilbert said the Australian government’s decision not to make her detainment public until 2019 led to her being sentenced to 10 years’ jail for espionage in a secret trial.

She hoped it would not be the same for Hiep.

“I would really hope that they would learn the lessons from that experience with that detention and apply them in order to act more expeditiously in [Hiep’s] case,” Moore-Gilbert said.

“Keeping that media spotlight on him will hopefully protect him a bit from some of the worst excesses of that regime.

“We need to put our foot down as a country … we really need to send a strong signal to Vietnam that [his arrest is] unacceptable and that we will accept nothing less than his immediate freedom.”

world.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
world.snippet: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers A controversial research trial ...
world.content:
A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.

It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.

Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.

Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.

The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.

The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.

The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.

In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.

Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.

According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.

The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.

“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.

Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.

The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.

Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.

This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”

When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.

Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

world.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
world.snippet: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza The Nobel peace...
world.content:
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.

Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.

“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”

In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.

“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.

“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”

Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.

The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.

Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.

The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.

The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.

“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.

Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa, home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.

“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.

Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.

“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.

In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.

“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.

Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.

On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

world.title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
world.snippet: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the f...
world.content:
Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.

The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.

In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.

Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.

The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.

In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

world.title: Egyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleagues
world.snippet: Matsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim Brotherhood Egyptian journalists...
world.content:
Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.

Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.

One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.

“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.

In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.

Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.

Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.

Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.

The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.

For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.

“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”

world.title: Scientists discover 180,000 giant tortoises on one Seychelles island
world.snippet: Free-roaming Aldabra population far exceeds human population of Seychelles after decades-long recovery programme A survey of the world’s ...
world.content:
A survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has discovered that the once endangered species is thriving.

A population of Aldabra giant tortoises lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.

The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island. This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.

The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022. It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.

Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.

Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, the CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.

In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island, but a recovery programme led to it becoming a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.

Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.

“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”

Despite the good news, the study’s authors say that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.

The study authors say invasive mammals remain a threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.

“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.

“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.

“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”
